title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he spent 20 years photographing the daily life of migrant workers
dek: Others photograph the era's anomalies; he insisted on photographing its everyday — eating, clocking in, learning English. When the 10,000-worker factory really did disappear, only a very few people had kept this archive.
why: Not an industry analysis — it's a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography for himself and his generation. The part in the second half about ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’ is the most valuable.
who: Founders and content people interested in the transformation of manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta factory era disappeared.
skip: The show preview and event announcements at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value unimportant
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process to make manufacturing more stable and make people more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean — anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. Though there were no machines to replace them yet, a person's value was already almost unimportant. This was his underlying motive for later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system that deliberately erases individual differences, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like getting into a bandit's den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The carriage was already full at the Wuchang starting station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed the glass with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. For more than thirty hours he couldn't sit, couldn't drink water; after getting off, his belly was terribly swollen. At the Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold like a piglet’ — first they took twenty-some yuan saying it was to Dongguan, then on the highway they demanded another ten for the expressway fee, and if you didn't pay, someone would come up and slap you, and finally they dumped you in a wasteland with no village ahead and no shop behind to change vehicles. He says he used the term for so many years, and only last year did he understand what it meant.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 it was very hard to find work; men had a much harder time than women. Factory recruitment notices directly stated they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring notice by National Highway 107; the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people started dropping, by 40 only ten or eight were left, by 50-some only he remained. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. After he got up they had him spar with someone; the other man did a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That's how he got his first job: security guard at a hotel gate, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he struggled with himself for a long time before buying his own camera: his salary was only about 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, well, if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing, and then another ten or twenty-some for enlargements — in that era it was a huge expense for him. At first he photographed factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war; instinctively he felt that photography was just about technique, about shooting clearly. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he discovered there was so much learning in photography, and he had no standard by which to measure it, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook; the first lesson was the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: The model contest photos got tens of millions of clicks, then he was told to delete them
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding a model contest; the women came onstage in swimsuits, evening gowns, and uniforms they had made, and there was also pole dancing. In 2008 he changed his position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — the models in front, the dense black mass of the audience in the distance — and sent the photos to Tencent right away; they went up on the portal site and got tens of millions of clicks in one morning. But online comments said this was choosing a mistress for the boss, a lover for the factory director; the public opinion was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete them. Tencent said they could only hide them; other sites' viral reposting couldn't be stopped, and in the end he was given a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: That photo of the female worker looking up — he originally didn't plan to use it
points.body: On January 5, 2011, as a senior supervisor, he entered the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. After two hours of work in the clean room there was a four-minute break; the place where they changed work clothes was hung all over with clean-room garments no one was wearing, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow townsman heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the experience people told him when he was learning photography was that ‘photos where the subject looks at the lens are not good photos’, so he never used this one. Later, Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organized the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and it was unexpectedly put on the front page. He later looked at the photo seriously and admitted it had its own appeal — different readers would have different spiritual responses, so a photographer should interpret his photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his work years were zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people weren't wanted, Henan people weren't wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories' information was independent, there was no networked computer system, and the social security system didn't require contributions, so this set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system didn't recognize it — the ID number was the same, the name was the same, the household registration address was the same, and the enterprise felt you were dishonest, so it zeroed out your work years. He says this won't do; our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those many years of work are real. When even present life has no security, it's simply impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years from now.

points.h: Density: he photographed for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photos around the thread of dense migrant-worker life, and won the excellence award and the Alpa award at the third Hard Instant Image Awards. Workers' gatherings shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung all over with clothes, from a distance airtight; and workshop switches, key cabinets, storage lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures creating a visual sense of density. He says at first it was unconscious; he shot with his phone every day, shot when organizing security guard training, shot when he randomly saw a fellow worker on the road, and it accumulated day by day, on and off for almost 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he hadn't observed in that way, and as a result, once he discovered it, it was so terrifying — even switches looked so spectacular.

points.h: Time as the warp, space as the weft, a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The complete thread he worked out was: time as the warp, space as the weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, the impact of capital on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a comprehensive three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text, and physical objects. Later he changed methods: starting from the keyword ‘migrant work’, he found ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related words on Baidu, got 322, went to Baidu Images and began screenshotting them all — this is the internet's understanding of migrant work, to be presented together with his own understanding from actually photographing, in one huge exhibition space. He says this is us watching the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compares himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers get the credit, but the ones carrying the loads are the Sherpas; I'll just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets being transported; later it referred to being cheated by middlemen and drivers who jack up the price layer by layer on the way to work.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to, rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally renowned photography agency; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers on its website one by one.
A photography award organized by Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China; Zhan Youbing once submitted and had his work shown on the front page.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it wasn't like you got on a bus — you felt like you'd gotten into a bandit's den.
This is this era: we watch the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we arrive at certainly won't be bad; but if we can only see society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
